passage:
Rashmi: Abhi says headache again. no football practice today either
Jeevan: third time this week. should I call the coach and say he's unwell?
Rashmi: I already told his class teacher he'd skip the trip. easier than a fight
Jeevan: we've been saying 'easier' a lot
Rashmi: I know 😔 last month it was just the quiz. now it's practice, the trip, his cousin's birthday
Jeevan: if we keep covering, he'll never find out he can cope
Rashmi: I don't want to drag him either. he looked so scared this morning
Jeevan: not drag. what if I walk him to the ground and he just watches the first 15 min? he decides after that
Rashmi: and we tell him we're proud he went, whatever happens
Jeevan: ok. I'll talk to him tonight, calmly
Rashmi: 🙏

qa.q: How many times this week has Abhi missed practice, according to Jeevan?
qa.a: Jeevan says it is the third time this week.

qa.q: What is Rashmi worried about when saying Abhi looked so scared?
qa.a: Rashmi is worried that pushing him would hurt him, even while seeing that covering for him has let his fear spread.

qa.q: What small step do Jeevan and Rashmi plan, and why is it better than rescuing or pushing?
qa.a: Jeevan will walk Abhi to the ground to watch the first fifteen minutes and let him decide, with praise for going; it builds courage gently without forcing or shielding.

qa.q: What might Abhi be experiencing as Rashmi and Jeevan keep accepting the headaches?
qa.a: Abhi probably feels quick relief each time, but with every missed event the next one is likely to feel scarier.

grounding: It shows two adults noticing that accepting excuses has fed Abhi's fear and choosing a kind, small step instead of rescuing or pushing.

passage:
For a month Saurabh had closed his hardware shop at four to drive Sonali to tuition on his scooter. She said the bus was too crowded, and it was easier than arguing. Before that she had skipped the district science fair, and then the temple fair, which she used to love.
On Tuesday a customer grumbled at the shut shutter, and Saurabh suddenly saw how big the fear had grown, with his help.
That evening he said, 'Tomorrow I'll walk you to the bus stand. Just one stop, to the post office. I'll be waiting there on the scooter.'
Sonali's face went pale. 'Papa, what if...'
'If it's too much, you get off. Either way, you tried.'
On Wednesday she rode one stop, gripping the rail. When she stepped down, he was there, grinning.

qa.q: What time had Saurabh been closing his shop?
qa.a: He had been closing it at four.

qa.q: What does Sonali's pale face and 'Papa, what if...' reveal?
qa.a: It shows she is frightened of the bus and already imagining things going wrong before she has even tried.

qa.q: What changed in Saurabh's approach, and why does it help more than driving her?
qa.a: Instead of rescuing her every day, he offers one short stop with himself waiting at the end, so Sonali faces a small piece of the fear and learns she can cope.

qa.q: How might Sonali feel when she steps down and sees her father grinning?
qa.a: She likely feels shaky but proud and relieved, finding out that one stop was something she could manage.

grounding: It shows a father realising his daily rescue has fed his daughter's avoidance and switching to a kind, small step.

passage:
For a month Ines had accepted every excuse. Abebe had a headache on the day of the class trip to Sintra. He was "too tired" for his friend's birthday. He wanted to skip football because "the coach is annoying". Each time she said, "Okay, stay home," partly because arguing upset him so much and partly because the house was calmer.
Then on Friday he asked her to phone the pharmacy for him, something he used to do easily. Her stomach sank. The excuses weren't about headaches. His world was shrinking, and she had been helping it shrink.
That evening she didn't push and didn't rescue. She sat on his bed. "I think things feel scary lately. I'm not going to make you do everything. But let's pick one small thing this week. You choose."
Abebe was quiet for a long time. "Maybe football. Just the warm-up."
"Just the warm-up," she agreed. "I'll wait in the car."

qa.q: What did Abebe ask Ines to do for him on Friday?
qa.a: Phone the pharmacy for him.

qa.q: What did Ines feel when Abebe asked her to phone the pharmacy?
qa.a: She felt a sinking worry, realising the excuses hid fear and that her kindness had been helping his world shrink.

qa.q: Why is Ines's new approach better than pushing or rescuing?
qa.a: She acknowledges the fear and invites one small, chosen step, so Abebe builds courage without being forced or shielded.

qa.q: What might Abebe be feeling when he chooses the warm-up?
qa.a: He likely feels nervous but a little relieved, since the step is small and he got to choose it.

grounding: A mother notices she has been accepting excuses and accommodating her son's fear, and shifts to kindly encouraging one small step.

passage:
In the school counsellor's small office, Naveen sat on a plastic chair and listed it all: Jaya had missed the science exhibition, the Annual Day rehearsal and two class tests this term. Each time she'd had a stomach ache, and each time he or her mother had written a note.
"She gets so upset," he said. "Honestly, it was easier."
The counsellor nodded. "That's very common. Parents want to protect. But each time she avoids, the fear grows a little."
Naveen looked at his hands. He remembered Jaya at eight, singing on stage, and felt a sharp stab of guilt.
Together they made a plan. No more notes for stomach aches unless the doctor advised it. Instead, small steps: Jaya would sit the next test but could take a seat near the door. Naveen would drive her and wait in the car park the first week, then only drop her off.
Walking out, he felt nervous, but clearer than he had in months.

qa.q: What did Jaya miss this term?
qa.a: The science exhibition, the Annual Day rehearsal and two class tests.

qa.q: What did Naveen feel remembering Jaya singing on stage at eight?
qa.a: He felt a sharp stab of guilt, seeing how the easy notes had helped her fear grow.

qa.q: What makes the new plan wise?
qa.a: It stops rescuing with notes but offers kind, small steps, like a seat near the door and a waiting father at first, so Jaya builds confidence.

qa.q: What might Jaya feel when she hears the plan?
qa.a: Jaya may feel scared and a bit upset, but also safer knowing her father will be close at first.

grounding: A father realises he has accommodated his daughter's fear with notes, and with a counsellor plans kind, small steps instead.

passage:
Dear Chandrika,
I'm writing because when we talk, I either say too much or nothing.
Over the last months I've said yes every time you wanted to skip something: the class picnic, your cousin's engagement, the badminton trials. I told myself I was keeping the peace. Truthfully, I didn't want to see you upset, and I didn't want to be the bad guy. But I've watched the list of places you can go get shorter, and I think my yeses helped make it shorter.
I'm not going to drag you anywhere. That wouldn't help either. But I'd like us to try one small thing each week, something you pick. Maybe it's just coming with me to the market on Sunday and buying the vegetables yourself. If it's hard, tell me, and we'll still count it as a try.
I'm proud of how hard you're working at this, even when it doesn't look like it.
Your Papa,
Ramesh

qa.q: What did Chandrika skip?
qa.a: The class picnic, your cousin's engagement, the badminton trials.

qa.q: What does Ramesh admit feeling about his yeses?
qa.a: He feels regretful and worried, recognising that avoiding conflict and upset helped Chandrika's world shrink.

qa.q: What does Ramesh propose, and why is it balanced?
qa.a: One small, chosen step each week, like buying vegetables at the market, which neither forces nor shields.

qa.q: What might Chandrika feel reading the letter?
qa.a: Chandrika may feel embarrassed but understood, relieved that Papa won't force anything and still believes in Chandrika.

grounding: A father admits that accepting his child's excuses accommodated the fear, and offers kind, chosen small steps instead.

passage: Gargi stirred her tea and spoke to her old college friend on the balcony. "It's Trisha. First she missed the inter-school quiz, a headache. Then her cousin's engagement. Then the class picnic. Every time, I said, fine, stay home, because if I pushed she'd cry, and the house would be tense all evening. Her father even started calling the school to say she was unwell. I told myself I was being kind. Last month her best friend stopped calling. And I realised I've been helping the fear, not Trisha. So last Sunday I tried something else. I said, 'You don't have to go to the whole birthday lunch. Just come with me for twenty minutes. If it's too much, we'll leave together.' She went pale, but she came. We stayed thirty. I told her I was proud of her for trying. I'm Gargi, and I'm learning that shielding her isn't the same as helping."

qa.q: How long did Gargi and Trisha stay at the birthday lunch?
qa.a: They stayed thirty minutes.

qa.q: What was Gargi feeling when she let Trisha stay home each time?
qa.a: Gargi felt worried and wanted to keep the peace, but she now feels uneasy and a little guilty, seeing that saying yes each time was helping the fear.

qa.q: What changed in Gargi's approach, and why is it likely to help?
qa.a: Instead of rescuing Trisha or pushing her, Gargi offered a small, time-limited step with a way out, then praised the effort, which builds Trisha's belief she can cope.

qa.q: What might Trisha be experiencing when she goes pale but comes anyway?
qa.a: Trisha is probably frightened, yet trusting Gargi's promise to leave together lets her try, and staying longer may leave her quietly proud.

grounding: Shows a parent who has been accepting excuses and accommodating a teen's fear, then kindly encouraging a small step instead of rescuing her.
